name: Meiji Restoration
title: The story of the Meiji Restoration

text: More than 170 years ago, Japan was governed by the shōguns of the Tokugawa family, and lords ran their own lands.
Many people went hungry, and samurai, who were paid in rice, fell into debt.
src: Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the 15th and last Tokugawa shōgun / the Tokugawa shogunate left the daimyō to run their own domains
Famine and unrest spread in the 1830s and 1840s / Samurai on fixed rice stipends fell into debt

text: For a long time Japan was closed, and only Dutch traders could come, at a place called Dejima.
Then American warships led by Matthew Perry arrived and made Japan open two ports.
src: the policy of sakoku had kept Japan closed, with only the Dutch trading at Dejima
Commodore Matthew C. Perry’s American expedition reached Japan in 1853 and returned with large warships to conclude the Convention of Kanagawa in 1854, which opened Shimoda and Hakodate

text: Some young samurai, called shishi or "men of spirit", wanted to give power back to the Emperor.
Two strong regions, Satsuma and Chōshū, joined together against the shōgun.
src: many lower and middle-ranking samurai became shishi, “men of spirit”, devoted to the Emperor / the return of political power to the Imperial Court
Led by Satsuma and Chōshū, an alliance of domains overthrew the shogunal system

text: More than 150 years ago, the teenage Emperor Meiji declared that power was his again.
The last shōgun had already given up his power, but a war was fought before his side gave in.
src: Emperor Meiji, the teenager Mutsuhito / on 3 January 1868 Emperor Meiji declared political power restored to the Imperial House
Tokugawa Yoshinobu, the 15th Tokugawa shōgun, gave up his powers / the Boshin War ended Tokugawa resistance

text: The new government ended the samurai class, and every man now had to serve in the army.
Some samurai, led by Saigō Takamori, rebelled, but the new army defeated them.
src: The new government abolished the domains and the samurai class / Conscription from 1873 made every man serve four years from the age of 21
the Satsuma Rebellion led by Saigō Takamori, put down by the new Imperial Japanese Army

text: Japan built schools, factories and shipyards, and sold silk to pay for machines.
Its new constitution, a set of rules for running the country, lasted until after the Second World War.
src: Raw silk became the chief export and paid for machinery / the state built shipyards, iron smelters and spinning mills / The state built a national system of free public schools
the Meiji Constitution of 1889 remained in place until the Allied occupation after the Second World War
